t: The epic grew from five Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, into an Akkadian epic whose Old Babylonian version dates to the 18th century BCE and whose Standard Babylonian version was compiled by Sîn-lēqi-unninni.

It tells of Gilgamesh's friendship with the wild man Enkidu, their killing of Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, Enkidu's death, and Gilgamesh's failed search for eternal life, which brings him to Utnapishtim, survivor of the flood.

Recovered from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh in the 1850s, it has been compared with the Genesis flood narrative, with Homer and with the Alexander legends, and new fragments are still being joined to it.
dyk: Before the cuneiform signs of his name could be pronounced accurately, Gilgamesh was first reintroduced to the modern world as “Izdubar”.
ev: Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, are composed, some perhaps as early as the Third Dynasty of Ur
The Old Babylonian version, Surpassing All Other Kings, is the first surviving version of the combined epic in Akkadian
Sîn-lēqi-unninni compiles the twelve-tablet Standard Babylonian version, He Who Saw the Deep, from earlier texts
Some of the best copies of the Standard Babylonian version are kept in the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh
Hormuzd Rassam finds the Standard Babylonian version in the ruins of the library of Ashurbanipal
George Smith reads translated fragments of the epic before the Society of Biblical Archaeology
Andrew George publishes his two-volume critical edition with Oxford University Press
The Gilgamesh Dream Tablet, seized by US officials in 2019, is returned to Iraq

f.made: Mesopotamian scribes: five Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh, some perhaps from the Third Dynasty of Ur; an Akkadian combined epic in its Old Babylonian version; and the Standard Babylonian version compiled from earlier texts by Sîn-lēqi-unninni, thought to have lived between 1300 and 1000 BCE.
f.form: An epic poem in Akkadian, with Sumerian forerunners, written in cuneiform on clay tablets; the Standard Babylonian version runs to twelve tablets, of which about two-thirds have been recovered, and uses much parallelism across two or three adjacent lines.
f.where: Tablets and fragments from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, studied at the British Museum; Old Babylonian tablets named after where they are kept or were found, such as the Pennsylvania, Yale and Sippar tablets; the Gilgamesh Dream Tablet, returned to Iraq in 2021.
f.known: the friendship of Gilgamesh and Enkidu; the killing of Humbaba in the Cedar Forest; the Bull of Heaven; Gilgamesh's quest for eternal life; Utnapishtim's account of the flood; the plant of youth stolen by a serpent; parallels with the Genesis flood narrative
